body_html:
How to think about it

A bar magnet behaves like a solenoid: its field lines are closed loops, so the net flux through any closed surface is zero and there are no magnetic monopoles. A magnetic dipole of moment m feels a torque mB sin θ and has potential energy −mB cos θ in a field.

Materials respond differently: diamagnetic substances (bismuth, copper, water) have small negative susceptibility; paramagnetic ones (aluminium, oxygen) small positive susceptibility that falls with temperature (Curie's law); ferromagnetic ones (iron, cobalt, nickel) are strongly magnetised and become paramagnetic above the Curie temperature.

Example

m = 2 A m², B = 0.5 T, θ = 90°. τ?

mB

Answer: 1 N m

Example

Copper is?

χ small, negative

Answer: diamagnetic

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a magnet cut in half gives separate poles.
  • Saying copper is paramagnetic.
  • Forgetting the minus sign in U = −mB cos θ.

faq.q: Why are there no magnetic monopoles?
faq.a: Every magnet, however small, has both a north and a south pole; magnetic field lines form closed loops.

faq.q: What happens to a ferromagnet above its Curie temperature?
faq.a: Its domains break up and it becomes paramagnetic.
